questions.question: After visiting young Jesus in Matthew 2, why do the wise men avoid going back to King Herod?
options: God warns them in a dream
Roman soldiers block the main road
Herod leaves Jerusalem for a war
A heavy snowstorm closes the pass
questions.explanation: Herod pretended he wanted to worship the child while plotting murder, so a dream warned the wise men to return home by another route.

questions.question: In Matthew 5, what does Jesus say is the real root behind murder?
options: Weak courts that let criminals go
Nursing bitter anger and insulting people
Lack of guards at city gates
Borrowing money you cannot pay back
questions.explanation: Jesus strips away the comfort of mere technical rule-keeping, showing that nursing rage and dehumanizing people with insults comes from the same root as violence.

questions.question: In Matthew 6, what is the only reward for people who pray loud in public for attention?
options: Forgiveness for their past money debts
Freedom from paying the temple tax
The human applause they wanted
A top seat on the council
questions.explanation: In Matthew 6:2-5, Jesus exposes showy religion as a transaction for clout: if you do good deeds for an audience, their applause is your entire payout.

questions.question: In Matthew 7, what must you do before fixing a tiny speck in a friend's eye?
options: Ask the local priest for permission
Pay off all your household debts
Wait seven days before speaking up
Pull the big plank from yours
questions.explanation: Jesus warns against using hyper-criticism of others' minor flaws to avoid facing our own massive blind spots.

questions.question: After a king forgives a servant's huge debt in Matthew 18, how does that servant treat a peer?
options: Chokes him over a tiny debt
Forgives the small debt right away
Hires him to work the fields
Shares half his remaining food
questions.explanation: Matthew 18:28-30 exposes a brutal hypocrisy: people who gladly accept massive grace for themselves often enforce ruthless accounting on everyone else.

questions.question: After Jesus fasts forty days in the wilderness, the tempter challenges him to turn stones into bread, jump from the temple pinnacle, and bow for global political power. What common thread defines how Jesus shuts down all three offers?
options: He debates the tempter by proving that physical hunger and earthly kingdoms are illusions
He refuses to use his authority for personal relief, public spectacle, or shortcuts around suffering
He summons angels immediately after the first challenge to end the confrontation by force
He agrees to perform the signs later in Jerusalem once his disciples are gathered to witness them
questions.explanation: Each temptation offers a real-world shortcutâ€”instant physical relief, viral spectacle to force belief, or raw political leverageâ€”and Jesus rejects all three by anchoring to foundational covenant boundaries.

questions.question: In Jesus' parable of the wheat and the weeds, why does the landowner forbid his field hands from ripping out the toxic weeds as soon as they spot them?
options: Because the weeds will naturally turn into wheat if given enough water and sunlight
Because the field hands were secretly the ones who planted the weeds at night
Because aggressive, premature purges end up tearing out the healthy roots alongside the bad
Because local agricultural law forbade harvesting anything before the autumn festival
questions.explanation: In Matthew 13:29, the owner recognizes that zealots trying to purify a mixed community too early lack the discernment to separate intertwined roots without destroying the good crop in the process.

questions.question: Moments after Peter is praised as 'the rock' for recognizing who Jesus is, what causes Jesus to turn around and call Peter a stumbling block?
options: Peter demands to be paid a salary as the head of the twelve disciples
Peter falls asleep while standing guard outside the camp at Caesarea Philippi
Peter refuses to share food with the Gentile crowds across the border
Peter pulls Jesus aside to scold him for saying his mission requires suffering and execution
questions.explanation: Peter wants a Messiah who wins through dominance, not sacrifice; when he tries to protect Jesus from the cross, Jesus exposes it as setting his mind on human ambition rather than God's purpose.

questions.question: In the parable of the vineyard workers, the laborers hired at dawn receive the exact full day's wage they agreed to. Why do they turn furious at the end of the day?
options: The landowner pays the exact same full day's wage to workers who only clocked in for the final hour
The landowner deducts the cost of their tools from their final payout
The foreman delays their payment until the following week
The landowner forces them to harvest an extra field after sunset without overtime
questions.explanation: They weren't cheated out of a single coin, but watching latecomers receive equal generosity triggered status envyâ€”proving how quickly comparison turns gratitude into resentment.

questions.question: In the parable of the talents, three servants are entrusted with capital while their master travels. Why is the third servant condemned when the master returns?
options: He embezzled the funds to buy personal land and lied about the accounting
He buried the money in the dirt out of fear-driven paralysis and blamed the master's harshness
He invested the money in a high-risk venture that went bankrupt during a famine
He gave the entire sum away to strangers without getting a receipt
questions.explanation: Notice the third servant didn't steal the moneyâ€”he simply froze out of fear of failure, hid behind a cynical view of his master, and treated inaction as safety.

questions.question: In Matthew 11, John the Baptist sends word from Herod's prison asking if Jesus is truly the Messiah, since Jesus is healing the sick rather than swinging the fiery axe of judgment John predicted in chapter 3. How does Jesus diagnose the generation watching both of them?
options: They sincerely misunderstood the prophetic timeline because the scribes had hidden the scrolls of Isaiah from the common synagogues in Galilee
They eagerly embraced John's call to fasting in the desert but rejected Jesus because he refused to validate the oral traditions of the Jerusalem elders

They act like spoiled children in a marketplace who reject John's strict asceticism as demonic and dismiss Jesus' table fellowship with outcasts as gluttony, using opposite excuses to avoid repentance
They demanded that John and Jesus unite their followers into a single military coalition before they would pledge allegiance to either teacher
questions.explanation: In Matthew 11:16-19, Jesus exposes how a cynical audience rigs the game: when John fasted, they called him crazy; when Jesus feasted with sinners, they called him compromisedâ€”proving their objections were just alibis for refusal.

questions.question: Matthew 15 places two scenes back to back: Jerusalem Pharisees attacking Jesus because his disciples eat with unwashed hands, followed by a Canaanite mother in Tyre begging for crumbs of mercy for her daughter. What structural irony connects these two encounters?
options: The disciples defend the Canaanite woman against the Pharisees, proving they have finally outgrown the tribal prejudices they showed earlier in Galilee
The Pharisees eventually repent after watching the Canaanite woman's humility, realizing that the purity laws were never meant to apply outside the borders of Judea
Both the Pharisees and the Canaanite mother attempt to manipulate Jesus through flattery, forcing him to withdraw from public ministry until the Passover festival

The insiders use pious 'Corban' vows as a legal loophole to dodge caring for their own parents while obsessing over external hand-washing, whereas the pagan outsider absorbs every test with fierce humility and is praised for great faith
questions.explanation: Matthew contrasts clean hands with corrupt hearts (15:1-20) against an 'unclean' Gentile outsider whose relentless, unpretentious trust wins the exact commendation the religious elite lacked (15:21-28).

questions.question: In Matthew 23, Scribes and Pharisees build lavish monuments to dead prophets while claiming, 'If we had lived in our ancestors' days, we would never have helped shed the prophets' blood.' How does Jesus turn this self-congratulatory nostalgia against them?
options: He warns that honoring safely dead truth-tellers costs nothing, while their active plot to kill the living prophet standing in front of them proves they share their ancestors' exact predatory DNA
He commands them to tear down the tombs of the prophets immediately because stone monuments violate the second commandment against carved images
He argues that their ancestors were actually innocent bystanders misled by foreign kings, making the current generation far less culpable than they claim
He commends their meticulous tithing of mint, dill, and cumin as sufficient compensation for their ancestors' historical failures
questions.explanation: In Matthew 23:29-32, Jesus diagnoses a timeless institutional delusion: institutions love to canonize dead reformers who can no longer inconvenience them while persecuting the living ones who challenge their power today.

questions.question: In Matthew 26, Peter swears he will die before denying Jesus, draws a sword in Gethsemane when soldiers arrive, yet hours later curses and denies knowing Jesus before a servant girl. What psychological arc explains why Peter was brave against armed troops but folded before a servant?
options: Peter realized in the courtyard that Judas had already bribed the Roman cohort to spare the other eleven disciples if they publicly disavowed Jesus before sunrise

In the garden Peter was still acting out his heroic script of dying in a blaze of glory alongside a conquering Messiah, whereas in the courtyard Jesus' refusal to fight shattered Peter's framework and left him exposed to quiet social shame
Peter was following a prearranged signal from Jesus to infiltrate the high priest's household undercover so he could rescue him during the morning transfer to Pilate
Peter lost his nerve only after watching John and James sign a formal written recantation in front of Caiaphas and the elders
questions.explanation: Adrenaline-fueled bravado is easy when you expect a miraculous fight; once Jesus banned the sword and surrendered, Peter's self-image collapsed, leaving him defenseless against awkward peer pressure by a fire.

questions.question: Matthew 27 pairs two men trying to wash their hands of innocent blood: chief priests refusing to put Judas' returned thirty silver coins into the temple treasury, and Pontius Pilate washing his hands in water before the crowd. What moral blind spot do both actions share?
options: Both are attempting to delay the execution until King Herod arrives from Galilee to assume legal jurisdiction over the case
Both genuinely believe Jesus is guilty of treason against Rome but are bound by ancient treaties to show public reluctance before carrying out a capital sentence
Both use a meticulous technicalityâ€”a scruple over 'blood money' rules and a theatrical basin of waterâ€”to manufacture the illusion of clean hands while actively executing an innocent man
Both repent of their involvement before the crucifixion begins and attempt to bribe the Roman guards to release Jesus secretly
questions.explanation: In Matthew 27:6 and 27:24, both religious and political power brokers soothe their consciences with hollow procedural rituals while signing off on judicial murder.

questions.question: When a man with leprosy begs to be healed in Mark 1, how does Jesus cure him?
options: Sends him to wash in Jordan
Writes a prayer on a scroll
Tells the disciples to pray first
Reaches out and touches him directly
questions.explanation: Everyone else stayed far away from lepers to avoid becoming unclean, but Jesus reached out and touched the untouchable man, making him clean instead.

questions.question: When a storm hits their boat in Mark 4 while Jesus sleeps, what do the disciples shout?
options: Don't you care if we drown?
Why did we sail at night?
Help us bail out the water!
Turn the boat back to shore!
questions.explanation: Under panic, human nature quickly mistakes calm stillness for indifference ('Don't you care?').

questions.question: In Mark 8, what does Jesus say is a bad trade even if you gain the whole world?
options: Paying heavy taxes to keep it
Losing your own soul for it
Having rivals steal your gold away
Working all night without any rest
questions.explanation: Jesus frames the ultimate bad bargain in plain terms: winning every prize on earth while losing yourself is total bankruptcy.

questions.question: In Mark 9, what honest cry does a desperate father shout when asking Jesus to heal his son?
options: I have never doubted you once!
Punish your disciples for failing me!
I believe; help my unbelief!
Show me a miracle in heaven!
questions.explanation: Mark 9:24 shows that real trust isn't faking 100% certaintyâ€”Jesus honors the father who admits his faith and doubt are happening at once.

questions.question: In Mark 12, why does Jesus say a poor widow's two tiny coins beat every rich gift?
options: Her coins were rare antique silver
She prayed loud by the box
The rich used fake Roman coins
She gave everything she had left
questions.explanation: Jesus measures generosity not by the dollar amount, but by what stays in your pocketâ€”the rich gave spare change, while she gave all she had.

questions.question: When four friends dig through a house roof to lower a paralyzed man in front of Jesus, why does Jesus first tell the man his sins are forgiven before healing his legs?
options: To force the critics in the room to confront that his visible healing proves his invisible authority to forgive
Because he did not realize the man was physically paralyzed until the crowd pointed it out
Because local Capernaum custom required a verbal blessing before touching a sick person
To delay the crowd while his disciples cleared an exit path through the doorway
questions.explanation: Anyone can claim an unverifiable inner credential ('your sins are forgiven'), so Jesus links the invisible claim to an undeniable physical test ('stand up, take your mat, and walk').

questions.question: In a synagogue on the Sabbath, religious leaders watch closely to see if Jesus will heal a man's withered hand so they can accuse him. What griefs and angers Jesus before he heals the man?
options: That the man with the withered hand refused to ask for help out loud
That the leaders' stubborn loyalty to rule-keeping made them silent when asked if it is right to save life
That his own disciples were arguing about who should sit in the front row
That the synagogue ruler locked the doors to keep the poor outside
questions.explanation: Mark 3:4-5 shows bureaucratic hardness at its worst: when an institution cares more about catching a technical violation than relieving human suffering right in front of it, its moral compass is dead.

questions.question: After Jesus restores a violent, tormented man who lived in the tombs of the Gerasenesâ€”and a herd of two thousand pigs drowns in the lakeâ€”how do the local townspeople react?
options: They throw a feast to celebrate that their dangerous neighbor is finally sane and clothed
They bring every sick person in the region and ask Jesus to stay as their governor
They are seized with fear and beg Jesus to leave their territory because of the economic disruption
They arrest the herdsmen for failing to guard the livestock on the hillside
questions.explanation: Mark 5:15-17 exposes a chilling real-world calculation: the town preferred living next to a familiar human tragedy in the graveyard over dealing with a disruptive healer who upset their livestock economy.

questions.question: King Herod actually respects John the Baptist and protects him in prison. Why does Herod ultimately give the order to have John beheaded anyway?
options: He discovers a secret letter proving John is plotting a military coup with Rome's enemies
John refuses to perform a miracle for Herod's visiting generals
The Roman emperor threatens to strip Herod of his tetrarchy unless John is executed
He makes a reckless public oath at a banquet and is too afraid of losing face in front of his dinner guests to back down
questions.explanation: Mark 6:26 is a textbook study in cowardice disguised as power: Herod was deeply distressed, yet he murdered an innocent man because he was more terrified of looking weak in front of his banquet guests.

questions.question: A wealthy, morally disciplined man runs up to Jesus asking what he lacks for eternal life, having kept the commandments since youth. Why does he walk away grieving when Jesus tells him to sell his holdings and give to the poor?
options: Because his wealth wasn't just an asset he ownedâ€”it was the functional security he refused to trade away
Because he had already pledged his estate to the Jerusalem temple treasury
Because Roman law prohibited citizens from liquidating ancestral land
Because Jesus refused to let him say goodbye to his family first
questions.explanation: Mark 10:21 says Jesus looked at him and loved him before naming the one thing holding him hostage: his moral record was clean, but his net worth was his actual god.

questions.question: In Mark 7, Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem question why Jesus' disciples eat without performing ceremonial hand-washing. How does Jesus use their own 'Corban' vow practice to expose the moral bankruptcy of their tradition?
options: They charged poor Galilean pilgrims an exorbitant currency-exchange fee before allowing them to purchase ceremonial water jars in the temple courts

They allowed a person to declare their wealth 'dedicated to God' as a legal shelter that exempted them from supporting their aging parents, using pious tradition to nullify a core commandment of Moses
They secretly exempted wealthy Sanhedrin members from the Sabbath travel restrictions while prosecuting common laborers for carrying grain
They altered the text of Deuteronomy in the synagogue scrolls to remove the requirement of caring for widows and orphans
questions.explanation: In Mark 7:9-13, Jesus shows how religious bureaucracy invents pious-sounding loopholes ('Corban') that let people feel spiritually superior while abandoning basic human duty to their own parents.

questions.question: In Mark 8, right after the disciples fret over forgetting bread in the boat despite having watched Jesus feed both 5,000 and 4,000 people, Jesus heals a blind man at Bethsaida in two stagesâ€”first seeing people like 'walking trees,' then seeing clearly. Why does Mark place this unique two-stage healing right before Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi?
options: Mark is contrasting the slow healing of Gentiles in the northern territories with the instant healings experienced by faithful Israelites in Capernaum
The man at Bethsaida lacked sufficient faith during the first prayer, forcing Jesus to bring him outside the village walls away from the skeptical Pharisees

The two-stage healing acts as a living parable of the disciples' own partial sight: Peter is about to see clearly enough to name Jesus as the Messiah, yet remain blind to the fact that the Messiah must suffer and die
The two stages represent the transition from the old covenant priesthood of John the Baptist to the new prophetic ministry of the twelve apostles
questions.explanation: Mark 8:14-33 uses the two-touch healing as a structural hinge: the disciples are no longer totally blind, but they still see Jesus as a blurry political 'tree' until the cross brings full focus.

questions.question: In Mark 10, Jesus asks exactly the same questionâ€”'What do you want me to do for you?'â€”to two different parties: first to James and John (10:36), and moments later to blind Bartimaeus by the Jericho roadside (10:51). What contrast does Mark expose through their two answers?
options: The apostles refuse to answer out of embarrassment over their ambition, while Bartimaeus demands a seat at the Passover banquet in Jerusalem
James and John ask for the power to call down fire on Jericho, whereas Bartimaeus asks for enough silver to pay off his family's tax debt to Rome
Both James and John and Bartimaeus ask for political liberation from Herod, proving that no one in Judea understood Jesus' spiritual mission

The insider apostles use the question to lobby for throne-room status and dominance over their peers, while the blind beggar asks simply for sight and immediately follows Jesus on the road toward the cross
questions.explanation: By repeating the exact prompt ('What do you want me to do for you?') in Mark 10:36 and 10:51, Mark contrasts the spiritually blind insiders chasing rank with the physically blind outsider who sees what actually matters.

questions.question: In Mark 11, Mark 'sandwiches' Jesus clearing the temple courts directly between two halves of the story of a leafy fig tree that had zero fruit. How does the outer story of the fig tree explain what Jesus is doing inside the temple?
options: Just as the fig tree advertised figs from a distance with lush leaves while producing nothing, the temple complex was bustling with impressive religious commerce while failing to bear real covenant justice or welcome the nations
Jesus cursed the fig tree because local farmers were hoarding their harvest to drive up prices for poor Passover pilgrims arriving from Galilee
The fig tree represented the Roman occupation of Judea, which looked invincible on the outside but would soon wither under a military uprising
The disciples had eaten from the fig tree without paying the owner, prompting Jesus to demonstrate the strict consequences of breaking the law
questions.explanation: Mark's classic 'Markan sandwich' (11:12-14, 15-19, 20-21) makes the cursed fig tree an enacted prophecy: all foliage and zero fruit is the exact diagnosis of a temple turned into a high-margin den of robbers.

questions.question: At the crucifixion in Mark 15, the chief priests mockingly sneer, 'He saved others; he cannot save himself! Let the Christ come down from the cross now, that we may see and believe.' Yet when the Gentile Roman centurion watches Jesus die, he declares him the Son of God. Where is the deep irony in the priests' taunt and the soldier's confession?
options: The centurion only confessed Jesus after seeing an army of angels descend on Golgotha, whereas the chief priests had already returned to the temple for evening prayers

The priests' taunt is unintentionally trueâ€”because only by refusing to save himself could Jesus save othersâ€”and it is precisely his self-sacrificing death, not a flashy escape from the cross, that convinces a hardened Roman executioner
The chief priests secretly believed Jesus was the Messiah but were forced by Pontius Pilate to read a scripted condemnation in front of the crowd
The centurion was actually a secret disciple from Capernaum whose servant Jesus had healed earlier in his Galilean ministry
questions.explanation: Throughout Mark, no human calls Jesus 'Son of God' until a hardened Roman executioner sees *how* he diesâ€”proving that the cross itself, not coming down from it, is the ultimate revelation of his identity.

questions.question: In Luke 10, after two religious leaders pass a beaten man, who stops to save him?
options: A wealthy merchant from Jerusalem
A Roman captain on patrol
A despised outsider from Samaria
A shepherd watching nearby flocks
questions.explanation: By making a hated Samaritan the hero who pays the bill and crosses ethnic lines, Jesus destroys the lawyer's attempt to limit who counts as a neighbor.

questions.question: In Luke 10, why does Jesus gently correct Martha when she complains about her sister Mary?
options: Mary already finished her kitchen work
The disciples were supposed to cook
Guests only needed water and bread
Martha's anxious busyness made her resentful
questions.explanation: Luke 10:40-42 highlights a classic burnout trap: turning good hospitality into anxious, score-keeping busyness that misses the person right in front of you.

questions.question: In Luke 12, why is the rich man who builds bigger barns called a fool?
options: He hoards wealth but dies tonight
He builds on a flood plain
He plants only one crop type
He overpays the local barn builders
questions.explanation: The man treated full barns as permanent insurance against death, planning decades of comfort on the very night his life ended.

questions.question: In Luke 18, why does the tax collector walk home forgiven instead of the proud Pharisee?
options: He gives more money that day
He humbly begs God for mercy
He stands in the priest's court
He quits his job before sunset
questions.explanation: The Pharisee used prayer to brag about his superiority over others, while the tax collector honestly owned his need for mercy.

questions.question: In Luke 19, how does tax collector Zacchaeus prove his heart has truly changed?
options: Writes a letter to the elders
Burns his tax books in public
Pays back everyone he cheated fourfold
Buys new horses for the disciples
questions.explanation: Real change shows up in the bank account: Zacchaeus immediately gives half his wealth to the poor and pays back four times anything he stole.

questions.question: When Jesus speaks in his hometown synagogue in Nazareth, the crowd initially praises himâ€”until he reminds them that Elijah and Elisha helped foreign outsiders rather than Israelites. How does his hometown react?
options: They take up an offering to send missionaries to Syria and Sidon
They invite the Roman garrison commander to hear the rest of the sermon
They politely ask him to verify his scroll citations with the elders
They erupt in rage, drive him out of town, and try to throw him off the cliff
questions.explanation: People love a hometown hero as long as he validates their group privilege; the moment Jesus challenges their tribal entitlement, admiration flips into murderous rage in seconds.

questions.question: Simon the Pharisee invites Jesus to dinner but skips every basic courtesy, while a woman known as a sinner washes Jesus' feet with her tears. How does Jesus explain the massive contrast between the two?
options: People who think they have needed very little forgiveness show very little love
Public sinners are naturally more emotional than educated religious scholars
Simon was distracted by managing his household servants during the banquet
The woman was trying to buy social standing among the Pharisee's guests
questions.explanation: In Luke 7:47, Jesus links gratitude directly to self-awareness: Simon's moral superiority made him cold and stingy, while the woman who knew the weight of her debt poured out extravagant gratitude.

questions.question: In the parable of the Prodigal Son, after the reckless younger brother comes home broke and is welcomed with a feast, what reveals that the dutiful older brother was just as estranged from the father's heart?
options: He demands the remaining half of the estate in cash and moves to a neighboring town
He refuses to enter the party and bitterly complains that his years of slaving never earned him even a young goat
He hires local guards to arrest his younger brother for squandering family property
He secretly burns the fattened calf in the kitchen before it can be served
questions.explanation: In Luke 15:28-30, the older brother exposes his own transactional motive: he stayed home and followed every rule not out of love for his father, but as a joyless wage-earner keeping score.

questions.question: At the Last Supperâ€”mere minutes after Jesus announces that one of them is about to betray himâ€”what argument breaks out among the disciples around the table?
options: Who should guard the door against the temple police
Whether they should flee to Bethany or stay inside the city walls
Which of them should be reckoned the greatest in rank
Why Judas was allowed to dip his bread in the same dish
questions.explanation: Luke 22:24 is a stunning snapshot of human ego: in the middle of the gravest night in history, the twelve immediately pivot from 'Who is the traitor?' to 'Which of us is number one?'

questions.question: Two disillusioned disciples walking to Emmaus explain to a stranger that they had hoped Jesus was the one to redeem Israel before he was crucified. Why had their hope collapsed?
options: They had never heard the Old Testament prophecies about Moses and the prophets
They heard a rumor that the Roman governor had sealed all the roads out of Judea
They believed the other ten disciples had already surrendered to the high priest
They assumed a true Messiah would overthrow Rome immediately rather than suffer first as the prophets described
questions.explanation: Their expectations were built on a selective reading of victory without suffering; Jesus walks them through the whole storyline of Scripture to show why the cross was the mission, not a detour.

questions.question: In Luke 9, as Jesus sets his face toward Jerusalem, a Samaritan village refuses to host him, prompting James and John to ask if they should call down fire from heaven to incinerate the town (echoing Elijah in 2 Kings 1). How does their later mission in Acts 8:14-17 bring this moment full circle?
options: Jesus rebukes their vengeful zeal in Luke 9, and in Acts 8 the exact same apostle John travels back to Samaria with Peter to lay hands on Samaritan converts and pray for a very different kind of fireâ€”the Holy Spirit
John refuses to enter Samaria in Acts 8 out of lingering resentment, forcing Philip and Barnabas to lead the Samaritan mission without him
The Samaritan village in Luke 9 eventually surrenders to James and John after a three-year famine validates their prophetic warning
Jesus permits them to call down fire on an empty hillside outside the village as a warning, which later convinces the Samaritans to listen to Philip in Acts 8
questions.explanation: Luke crafts a brilliant two-volume character arc: the 'Sons of Thunder' who wanted to burn Samaria to the ground in Luke 9:54 return to Samaria in Acts 8:14-17 to welcome them as family.

questions.question: At a Sabbath dinner in the house of a prominent Pharisee in Luke 14, Jesus watches guests jockey for the VIP seats, tells the host to invite people who cannot pay him back, and answers a guest's pious toast with the parable of the Great Banquet. What social economy is Jesus dismantling across all three moments?
options: He prohibits his followers from owning private real estate, oxen, or family businesses, arguing that commercial trade is incompatible with entering the kingdom

He dismantles the ancient patronage system where hospitality was used as a status ladder and reciprocity ledger, showing that the people most confident of their seat at God's table will talk themselves out of it with respectable excuses
He instructs the Pharisees to abolish Sabbath meals altogether and replace them with silent fasting in the temple courts
He warns the host that Roman tax collectors are monitoring their dinner guest lists to assess higher tribute on wealthy Judean households
questions.explanation: Throughout Luke 14:7-24, Jesus exposes how elite dinner tables operate on ego and quid-pro-quo favors, warning that those preoccupied with their own fields, livestock, and social standing will miss the actual feast.

questions.question: In Luke 16, a fired estate manager scrambles to slash his master's debtors' bills before losing his job so those debtors will welcome him into their homes afterward. Why does the master commend the 'dishonest manager' for acting shrewdly?
options: The master was secretly testing whether the debtors would report the altered promissory notes to the local village elders
The manager was only cancelling his own illegal usury commission rather than the master's principal, making the transaction a model of strict Levitical accounting
He is not praising the manager's ethics, but his clear-eyed urgency: the manager faced his coming deadline without illusion and used temporary assets right now to secure relationships for his future
Jesus uses the parable as dark sarcasm to encourage his disciples to hoard silver before the Roman siege of Jerusalem begins
questions.explanation: In Luke 16:8-9, the point isn't dishonestyâ€”it's decisiveness: worldly operators recognize when their clock is running out and leverage everything they hold today for what comes next.

questions.question: In the parable of the rich man and Lazarus in Luke 16, the rich man never kicks or insults Lazarus at his gate, yet in Hades he still treats Lazarus as an errand boy ('send Lazarus to dip his finger in water... send him to my father's house') and insists a resurrection miracle would make his five brothers repent. How does Abraham expose the rich man's double delusion?
options: The rich man is condemned solely because he acquired his purple linen through fraudulent contracts with the Roman governor
Abraham explains that the five brothers have already donated the family estate to the poor after hearing John the Baptist preach at the Jordan River
Abraham tells him that Lazarus was actually a disguised angel sent to test the wealthy neighborhoods of Jerusalem before the Passover

The rich man knew Lazarus's name all alongâ€”proving his neglect was willful indifference, not ignoranceâ€”and Abraham points out that people who ignore Moses and the prophets in plain sight will rationalize away even someone rising from the dead
questions.explanation: Notice the chilling detail in Luke 16:24: the rich man knew Lazarus by name the whole time he stepped over him, and even in torment he still acts entitled and blames a 'lack of miracles' rather than a hardened heart (16:31).

questions.question: Unique to Luke's Gospel, Pilate sends Jesus to Herod Antipas, who is thrilled because he hopes to see Jesus perform a miracle like a court magician. When Jesus refuses to say a single word, what chilling political side effect occurs that day?
options: Jesus gives Herod absolute silence because Herod had already silenced John the Baptist and wanted entertainment rather than truth, and Herod and Pilateâ€”who had been bitter enemiesâ€”become friends over their shared mockery of him
Herod secretly offers to release Jesus if he agrees to relocate his followers to Galilee and stop criticizing the temple priesthood
Pilate reports Herod's interference to the Emperor Tiberius, triggering a border war between Judea and Galilee later that spring
Herod's court officials are so terrified by Jesus' silence that they resign their posts and join the disciples on the Mount of Olives
questions.explanation: Luke 23:8-12 captures two dark realities at once: truth refuses to perform tricks for a voyeuristic ruler who murdered John, and bitter political rivals quickly bond when they find a common scapegoat.

questions.question: At the wedding in Cana in John 2, what surprises the banquet master about the wine Jesus made?
options: It was served in gold cups
The best wine was saved last
The bride's father paid nothing
It came from a foreign country
questions.explanation: Normally hosts served the good wine first and brought out the cheap stuff later, but Jesus saved the best for last.

questions.question: In John 6, why does Jesus say the huge crowd chased him across the lake?
options: Rome paid them to spy
They forgot their baskets behind
They just wanted more free bread
Herod sent soldiers to arrest him
questions.explanation: In John 6:26, Jesus calls out the crowd's real motive: they wanted free food and political perks, not the truth.

questions.question: In John 8, who does Jesus say may throw the first stone at the accused woman?
options: Only the Roman governor Pilate
The witnesses who signed the paper
The oldest priest in the temple
Whoever has never sinned at all
questions.explanation: By turning the spotlight onto the accusers' own consciences, Jesus causes the entire mob to drop their stones and walk away.

questions.question: In John 12, why does Judas really complain when Mary pours expensive perfume on Jesus?
options: He steals from the money bag
He wants to impress the priests
He owes money to the merchant
He is jealous of Mary's gift
questions.explanation: John 12:4-6 notes that Judas hid his greed behind fake concern for the poor because he routinely stole from the group's money bag.

questions.question: In John 20, what convinces doubting Thomas that Jesus is truly alive again?
options: Peter reads a scroll from Isaiah
Jesus shows his nail-scarred hands
Roman guards admit the tomb opened
Bright lightning flashes over the house
questions.explanation: Thomas refused to believe secondhand reports until Jesus stood before him and invited him to inspect the scars on his hands and side.

questions.question: Nicodemus, a high-ranking Pharisee and member of the Jewish ruling council, seeks out Jesusâ€”but comes at night. What does Jesus immediately challenge in their conversation?
options: Nicodemus's refusal to pay the Roman tribute tax
Nicodemus's vote in the council to arrest John the Baptist
Nicodemus's assumption that his elite credentials and pedigree are enough without a total spiritual rebirth
Nicodemus's lack of knowledge of the Greek language
questions.explanation: Coming under cover of darkness to protect his institutional reputation, Nicodemus expects a polite peer-to-peer debate, but Jesus tells the credentialed insider he has to start over from scratch.

questions.question: At Jacob's well at noon, when Jesus gently reveals that he knows all about the Samaritan woman's five past husbands and current partner, what classic deflection move does she immediately try?
options: She drops her water jar and runs back into town without saying another word
She blames the local elders for refusing to grant her a legal divorce
She claims she is actually related to the town magistrate of Sychar
She pivots the conversation to a safe, abstract religious debate about which mountain is the right place to worship
questions.explanation: In John 4:19-20, the instant a conversation gets uncomfortably personal, she changes the subject to an ancient theological controversyâ€”a textbook human defense mechanism.

questions.question: By the pool of Bethesda, Jesus approaches a man who has been disabled for thirty-eight years and asks a seemingly obvious question: 'Do you want to get well?' How does the man initially respond?
options: Instead of saying yes, he recites his excuse about why no one ever helps him and others always cut in front of him
He shouts 'Yes!' and tries to crawl toward Jesus
He asks Jesus for silver coins rather than physical healing
He tells Jesus that the Sabbath rules forbid him from moving his mat
questions.explanation: After 38 years in the same spot, helplessness and grievance can become an identity; Jesus' sharp question cuts straight past three decades of blaming others to demand agency.

questions.question: When a man born blind is healed by Jesus on the Sabbath, the Pharisees interrogate the man, his parents, and the man a second time. Why do they ultimately throw him out of the synagogue?
options: Because he admits he made up the story to collect more alms at the gate
Because the undeniable evidence of his eyesight destroys their ideological premise, and he mocks their refusal to accept the facts
Because he refuses to pay the required temple purification fee
Because his parents testify that he was never actually blind
questions.explanation: John 9 is a masterclass in confirmation bias: when hard reality ('One thing I do know: I was blind but now I see') contradicts an institution's dogma, the institution expels the witness rather than admit error.

questions.question: Knowing that the Father had put all things under his power, what does Jesus immediately get up from the supper table and do in John 13?
options: He dictates the organizational hierarchy for the twelve apostles after his departure
He marches to the temple courts to confront the high priest Caiaphas
He wraps a towel around his waist and washes the dirty feet of his disciplesâ€”including Judas and Peter
He divides his possessions among his mother and brothers
questions.explanation: Notice the causal link in John 13:3-5: it isn't insecurity that makes someone serve; it is total security in who he is that frees Jesus to take the lowest servant's job in the room.

questions.question: After Jesus raises Lazarus from the dead in John 11, the panicked Sanhedrin warns that if everyone believes in him, 'the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation,' and High Priest Caiaphas argues it is better for one man to die for the people than for the whole nation to perish. Where is the layered irony in their calculation?
options: The Pharisees rejected Caiaphas's proposal on the spot and voted to offer Jesus a permanent seat on the council instead
Caiaphas was secretly a follower of Jesus who used reverse psychology to convince the Sadducees to delay the arrest until after the Passover festival
The Roman governor had already promised the Sanhedrin full independence if they handed over Lazarus and Jesus before the end of the month

On a political level, executing Jesus to appease Rome fails to prevent Rome from destroying their temple and nation in AD 70 anyway; on a theological level, Caiaphas's cynical realpolitik unintentionally states the exact substitutionary meaning of the cross
questions.explanation: John 11:48-52 highlights a double irony: their pragmatic sacrifice of an innocent man to save their political skin failed to save Jerusalem from Rome, while Caiaphas's ruthless slogan accidentally spoke the gospel truth.

questions.question: In John 18, the religious leaders refuse to step inside Pilate's palace so they can stay 'ceremonially clean' for Passover, and moments later they demand the release of Barabbasâ€”an armed insurrectionistâ€”so Jesus can be executed as a threat to Caesar. What dual contradiction does John expose here?
options: They obsess over avoiding external ritual defilement on a pagan floor while orchestrating a judicial murder, and they demand the release of an actual anti-Roman terrorist while accusing the peaceful Jesus of treason against Rome
They enter the palace only after Pilate agrees to wash the courtyard tiles with water brought from the pool of Siloam
Barabbas was actually a high-ranking Sadducee who had been arrested for refusing to pay the temple tax to Caiaphas
Pilate tricks them into violating the Passover rules by holding the trial after sunset on the Mount of Olives
questions.explanation: John 18:28-40 lays bare how completely hatred blinds moral reasoning: keeping external rules clean while plotting murder, and freeing a violent rebel while prosecuting Jesus as a rebel.

questions.question: In John 19, Pilate repeatedly tries to release Jesus until the crowd plays their trump card: 'If you release this man, you are not Caesar's friend,' culminating in the chief priests shouting, 'We have no king but Caesar!' Why is this shout the ultimate self-betrayal of the priests' own identity?
options: The chief priests were quoting an ancient proverb from the book of Daniel that commanded exiled Jews to honor foreign emperors above the law of Moses

To corner a nervous Roman bureaucrat into executing their rival, Israel's chief priests publicly renounce the core covenant confession that God alone is Israel's King and pledge total allegiance to a pagan emperor
Pilate had threatened to execute the entire Sanhedrin unless they signed a loyalty oath to Emperor Tiberius before noon
The crowd shouting in the courtyard consisted entirely of Roman soldiers dressed in civilian clothing to intimidate Pilate
questions.explanation: In John 19:12-15, Pilate thinks he is judging Jesus, but the trial actually judges Pilate (who trades justice for career safety) and the priests (who trade away Israel's covenant hope just to win an argument).

questions.question: Across John's Gospel, Nicodemus appears three times: coming to Jesus in the dark in chapter 3, cautiously asking the council for fair legal procedure in chapter 7, and hauling seventy-five pounds of burial spices in broad daylight after the crucifixion in chapter 19. What character paradox does his three-chapter arc trace?
options: The Sanhedrin officially commissioned Nicodemus and Joseph to bury Jesus quickly so the Roman soldiers would leave the city walls before Passover
Nicodemus brings the royal burial spices because he still believes Jesus will wake up inside the tomb and lead an armed revolt before the Sabbath ends

While the twelve vocal insiders who swore they would die for Jesus scatter when the crisis hits, two cautious secret insidersâ€”Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemusâ€”finally step into the light and risk their status when there is zero earthly advantage left to gain
Nicodemus only steps forward after Peter and John promise to appoint him head of the Jerusalem church in exchange for the burial plot
questions.explanation: John traces Nicodemus from night (3:2) to tentative twilight (7:50) to costly daylight loyalty (19:39): he comes out of hiding at the exact moment Jesus' cause looks 100% dead.

questions.question: In John 21, Jesus cooks breakfast for the disciples over a 'charcoal fire' (the only other place that specific Greek word appears in the New Testament is the courtyard fire where Peter denied him in 18:18), asks Peter three times if he loves him, and then tells Peter how he will die. When Peter immediately points at John and asks, 'Lord, what about him?', what human reflex is Jesus cutting off?
options: Jesus rebukes Peter for speaking to John because the two apostles had refused to speak to each other since the night of the arrest
Jesus reveals that John had secretly failed a similar test in Jerusalem and would therefore be demoted from leadership among the twelve
Peter was asking whether John should stay behind in Galilee to manage the fishing business while Peter traveled to Rome

After intentionally recreating the charcoal-fire scene of Peter's threefold failure to restore him, Jesus refuses to let Peter relapse into sideways comparison with a peer's calling: 'What is that to you? You follow me!'
questions.explanation: In John 21:9-22, Jesus heals Peter's past shame around a charcoal fire, but the moment Peter hears his future will be costly, his old competitive ego flares upâ€”and Jesus tells him to keep his eyes in his own lane.

questions.question: At the temple gate in Acts 3, what does Peter give the lame beggar instead of money?
options: Complete healing in Jesus' name
A warm coat and bread
A job cleaning the courts
A letter to the priests
questions.explanation: The beggar only hoped for a few copper coins to survive another day, but Peter gave him his legs back in Jesus' name.

questions.question: In Acts 4, why can't the council deny the miracle done by Peter and John?
options: Roman soldiers guard the fishermen
The healed man stands right there
Peter calls fire from heaven
Temple guards go on strike
questions.explanation: Institutional threats hit a brick wall when the forty-year-old man who had been crippled since birth is standing right next to them on his own two feet.

questions.question: In Acts 8, what mistake does Simon the Magician make when he sees the Spirit given?
options: Challenges Peter to a duel
Steals the church money bag
Tries to buy God's power
Demands to rule the city
questions.explanation: Simon treated spiritual power like a magic trick he could buy and sell for profit, earning a sharp rebuke from Peter.

questions.question: In Acts 12, when an angel frees Peter from prison, how does the church react?
options: Opens the gate right away
Runs to tell King Herod
Hides him in the cellar
Refuses to believe he's free
questions.explanation: In a funny moment of human nature, the church is earnestly praying for Peter's release yet tells the servant girl she is crazy when he actually knocks on the door.

questions.question: After an earthquake opens the Philippi jail in Acts 16, what stops the guard from killing himself?
options: Paul shouts nobody ran away
City judges pardon the guard
Silas grabs the guard's sword
Soldiers lock the outer gate
questions.explanation: Roman guards were executed if prisoners escaped; by staying inside the dark cell to save their jailer's life, Paul and Silas won his whole family.

questions.question: Ananias and Sapphira sell a piece of property and bring part of the money to the apostles. Since Peter explicitly tells them the land and the cash were 100% theirs to keep, what was their actual crime?
options: Failing to donate the mandatory 100% required of all church members
Conspiring to stage a fake display of total sacrifice to buy the same public prestige Barnabas had received
Selling property that legally belonged to the Jerusalem temple
Refusing to pay the Roman property transfer tax
questions.explanation: In Acts 5:4, Peter makes clear there was zero compulsory communismâ€”they could have kept every penny; what was lethal was faking radical generosity to purchase spiritual clout on a discount.

questions.question: When the furious council wants to execute the apostles in Acts 5, the respected Pharisee Gamaliel stands up and talks them down with what pragmatic historical argument?
options: Executing popular teachers during a festival will trigger a Roman military crackdown
The apostles should be exiled to Galilee where they have no political influence
If this movement is merely human, it will fizzle out like past rebellions; if it is from God, you cannot stop it and will only find yourselves fighting God
Jewish law requires a thirty-day cooling-off period before capital sentences
questions.explanation: Gamaliel uses calm historical realism to check institutional panic: fake movements collapse under their own weight, while truth doesn't needâ€”and can't be crushed byâ€”state violence.

questions.question: As the early Jerusalem church grows rapidly, Greek-speaking believers complain that their widows are being overlooked in the daily food distribution compared to the Hebrew-speaking widows. How do the apostles solve the crisis?
options: They tell the Greek-speaking families to stop complaining and trust the leadership
They shut down the food program entirely so they can focus on preaching
They divide the church into two separate congregations based on language
They acknowledge the operational gap and empower seven respected leaders from the neglected group itself to run the distribution
questions.explanation: Notice in Acts 6:5 that all seven men chosen to run the food distribution carry Greek namesâ€”the leaders didn't get defensive; they handed real authority directly to the underserved group.

questions.question: In Damascus, Ananias is told in a vision to walk over to Straight Street and lay hands on Saul of Tarsusâ€”the exact man who arrived in town with arrest warrants to haul believers away in chains. How does Ananias handle the assignment?
options: He voices his legitimate fear and the hard facts about Saul's reputation, then walks into the house and calls him 'Brother Saul'
He flees Damascus immediately, just as Jonah fled toward Tarshish
He sends a servant ahead to verify whether Saul is actually blind or setting a trap
He demands that the Jerusalem apostles come to Damascus first to vouch for Saul
questions.explanation: Acts 9:13-17 shows real courage: Ananias doesn't pretend Saul isn't dangerousâ€”he states his objection plainly, hears the mission, and walks straight into the room to greet his former persecutor as a brother.

questions.question: In Ephesus, a violent riot fills the theater with thousands chanting 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!' for two hours. How did Demetrius the silversmith actually start the riot behind closed doors?
options: By discovering that Paul's companions had defaced the temple of Artemis
By warning his fellow guild craftsmen that Paul's message was hurting their high-margin business selling silver shrines
By receiving a vision from the temple priestesses calling for a holy war
By protesting a new Roman tariff on imported silver ore
questions.explanation: Acts 19:24-27 pulls back the curtain on how public outrage is manufactured: behind the loud religious and patriotic slogans in the street was a trade union protecting its profit margin.

questions.question: In Acts 7, Stephen is put on trial before the Sanhedrin for allegedly speaking against the Jerusalem temple and the law of Moses. Instead of defending himself directly, why does Stephen spend fifty verses retelling the stories of Abraham in Mesopotamia, Joseph in Egypt, and Moses at the burning bush in Midian?
options: He attempts to prove to the Sadducees that he has memorized the entire Pentateuch in Hebrew rather than Greek
He stalls for time while the Greek-speaking believers evacuate Jerusalem ahead of Saul's temple police

He proves from their own Scriptures that God's presence was never boxed inside Jerusalem's stone templeâ€”appearing in Mesopotamia, Egypt, and Midianâ€”and that Israel's leaders had a recurring historical habit of rejecting the exact deliverers God sent them
He argues that the Jerusalem temple was legally invalid because King Solomon used foreign Phoenician builders from Tyre
questions.explanation: Stephen's speech in Acts 7 isn't a rambling history lessonâ€”it is a devastating legal brief proving two points: God is not geographically trapped in the temple building, and the council is repeating their ancestors' pattern of rejecting Joseph and Moses.

questions.question: In Acts 10, Peter is staying in Joppaâ€”the exact port where Jonah boarded a ship to flee from preaching to Gentile Ninevehâ€”when a rooftop vision commands him to eat unclean animals just before messengers arrive from the Roman centurion Cornelius. Why did God have to orchestrate Simultaneous visions for both Cornelius and Peter?
options: Because Cornelius refused to listen to Philip the Evangelist, who was already living in Caesarea, and demanded to speak only to the chief apostle
Because Roman military law prohibited centurions in Caesarea from inviting Jewish fishermen into their barracks without prior approval from the provincial governor
Because Peter had vowed at the Last Supper never to enter a Roman soldier's house after watching the cohort arrest Jesus in Gethsemane

Because centuries of ethnic and ritual separation were so deeply entrenched in Peter's conscience that even after three direct commands from heaven he was still baffled, requiring an undeniable collision of visions and the Spirit falling on Gentiles to break his prejudice
questions.explanation: From Joppa (reversing Jonah's flight), Peter has to be pried loose from a lifetime of 'clean vs. unclean' tribal conditioning (Acts 10:14, 28, 34) so the church can cross its biggest cultural barrier.

questions.question: Acts 15 records two very different conflicts in the exact same chapter: first, the Jerusalem Council debating whether Gentile converts must be circumcised to be saved, and immediately afterward, Paul and Barnabas splitting up over whether to take John Mark after his earlier desertion. What does the pairing of these two disputes reveal about early church leadership?
options: The leaders achieved Spirit-led unity when defending core gospel freedom for Gentiles, yet two faithful partners could still reach an irreconcilable practical disagreement over risk versus second chancesâ€”which God redeemed by multiplying one mission team into two
Barnabas secretly agreed with the circumcision party from Judea, using the dispute over his cousin John Mark as an excuse to break away from Paul's Gentile mission
The Jerusalem elders ordered Paul and Barnabas to separate so that neither apostle would accumulate too much authority over the churches in Syria and Cilicia
Paul admitted before leaving Antioch that his refusal to forgive John Mark violated the council's decree, prompting Silas to take over leadership of the trip
questions.explanation: Acts 15 refuses to sanitize reality: solving a massive doctrinal crisis (15:1-35) doesn't make leaders immune to sharp operational friction over personnel (15:36-40)â€”yet both Barnabas's restoration of Mark and Paul's mission bore lasting fruit.

questions.question: Compare Paul's sermon in the synagogue of Pisidian Antioch (Acts 13) with his address to the Stoic and Epicurean philosophers at the Areopagus in Athens (Acts 17). How does Paul completely re-architect his starting point for the Athenian audience while arriving at the exact same non-negotiable conclusion?
options: In Athens he avoids mentioning judgment or resurrection altogether so he can win an honorary seat on the Areopagus council first

In the synagogue he reasons from Israel's exodus, King David, and the prophets, whereas in Athens he cites zero Hebrew Scripturesâ€”starting instead from creation, an 'Unknown God' altar, and Greek poetsâ€”before confronting both audiences with the resurrection of Jesus
He denounces Greek poetry as demonic in Athens just as he denounced the law of Moses in Pisidian Antioch
He performs public exorcisms at the Parthenon because the Athenian philosophers refused to listen to logical arguments
questions.explanation: Paul never uses a one-size-fits-all script: with biblically literate listeners he starts with Scripture (Acts 13:16-41); with pagan philosophers he starts with creation and their own poets (Acts 17:22-31)â€”yet never waters down the resurrection.

questions.question: Across Acts 24â€“26, Roman governors Felix and Festus and King Agrippa all privately recognize that Paul has broken no Roman lawâ€”yet Felix leaves him in prison for two years hoping for a bribe and to 'do the Jews a favor,' and Festus tries to transfer him to Jerusalem where an ambush awaits. How does Paul use Roman law itself to turn their corrupt stalling into his ticket to Rome?
options: Paul convinces King Agrippa to overrule Festus's jurisdiction and appoint him as a diplomatic envoy to the Roman Senate
Paul pays the bribe Felix demanded using funds sent by the church in Philippi, securing a military escort to Italy

Recognizing that Festus is willing to trade a prisoner's life for political goodwill with Jerusalem's elite, Paul invokes his constitutional right as a Roman citizen to appeal directly to Caesarâ€”forcing the empire to fund and guard his journey to its capital
Paul stages a hunger strike in the Caesarea barracks until the centurion Julius agrees to smuggle him aboard a grain ship bound for Alexandria
questions.explanation: In Acts 25:9-12, Paul isn't naive about bureaucratic corruption: when Festus tries to use him as a political bargaining chip, Paul plays his Roman citizenship card ('I appeal to Caesar!') to fulfill his mission to reach Rome.
